tree.style: margin: 18px 0 0; font-size: 18px; line-height: 1.65; color: #40514a; text-wrap: pretty;

tree: In a property office, the person who picks up is rarely the person who can help. Callers get passed around, put on hold, or transferred to someone who already left for a showing.

tree: Routing sends each call to the teammate who handles that reason, checks whether they’re available first, and uses a fallback when they’re not.

tree: What happens if the assigned teammate is unavailable?
The call goes to the fallback you set, such as the next available teammate, an office manager, or voicemail with a callback task. The caller is never left ringing.

tree.style: border: 1px solid rgba(16,32,26,.1); border-radius: 14px; padding: 20px 22px; background: #fff;

tree: Can calls be routed by reason or department?
Yes. Callers choose a reason, and each reason maps to a team or person. Rules can also differ by time of day.

tree.style: border: 1px solid rgba(16,32,26,.1); border-radius: 14px; padding: 20px 22px; background: #fff;

tree: The teammate sees who is calling and why before they answer, so the caller doesn’t have to repeat themselves.

tree.style: border: 1px solid rgba(16,32,26,.1); border-radius: 14px; padding: 20px 22px; background: #fff;

tree: Who should use call transfer and routing?
Multi-person offices, property managers, service companies and support desks where different people handle different questions.

tree.style: border: 1px solid rgba(16,32,26,.1); border-radius: 14px; padding: 20px 22px; background: #fff;

tree: Yes. Each call record shows the route taken, who answered, any fallback used and the outcome.
